goal_cards.private_goal: Make sure a small town can still get a road built.
Keep enough tax money in the city to run the buses.
Get a say in something, even though you can't vote.
Keep the rules simple enough to follow without a lawyer.
Make sure nobody can vote away how your family worships.
Get schools funded the same in every town.

letters.body: Our school closed the library this year. The town next to ours built a new gym. My teacher says it's because of how the money works. I don't understand why we're different.
We got the library back. It's not big but there's a librarian on Tuesdays and Thursdays now. My teacher says the state had to send money because of the rule you wrote.
Two thousand of us signed a petition about the water. We were told signatures don't do anything here — only the legislature can start a law. I'm not sure what the signatures were for.
The water measure made the ballot. We didn't win, but it was on there, and 40,000 people had to think about it. That's more than happened in the twelve years before.
I have to raise money to keep my seat. Last month a lawyer who gave to my campaign appeared in my courtroom. I sent the case to another judge, but I think about it.
A commission picked the judge in my case and I never got to vote on him. When I asked how to get rid of a bad judge, nobody could give me a straight answer.
My class had an idea for a park cleanup day. We wrote to the lawmakers. They never wrote back. There was nothing else we could do.
My class got 500 people to sign our park paper. Now the whole town gets to vote on it. My name is on the first page.
We voted for our judge. The judge with the most yard signs won. I don't know if signs make you fair.
Experts picked our judge this year. My mom never got a say. She wants to know who picked the experts.
Our school shares one art teacher with two other towns. The town next door has a pool. My dad says it's about the money rules.
Our school got new books this year. My teacher says the state helped pay because of the rule. The pool town got the same books too.
I rent my home. I do not own land. Under this rule I would never get to vote. My boss would.
I just turned 18. I voted for the first time on Tuesday. I did not need to own anything. I just needed to be me.
I teach at the school in this town and rent my apartment. Under this rule my landlord can vote and I can't. What does owning land have to do with having a say?
I'm the first in my family to vote. My grandmother told me the rules used to keep people like us out. She came with me to watch.
Our school board rule changed because 51 percent of voters wanted it. My mom says that is how it should work. My neighbor says a rule that thin can flip back next year.
We got 55 percent and still lost. The measure needed 60. I understand the reason, but it is strange to win the vote and lose the question.
Our town voted to build a skate park. It won by a little. My friend says a small win still counts. I think she is right.
Our skate park vote got more yes than no. It still did not pass. The rule said we needed way more than half.

reflections.prompt: What would you do if the lawmakers said no to your idea?
What did the other side say that made the most sense to you?
What makes a judge fair? Talk it over.
Can a judge be fair if they have to win votes? Can experts be fair if nobody voted for them?
Is it fair if one school has more than another? Why or why not?
Who should pay for a school in a town with very little money? Say your reason out loud.
Why should every grown-up get a vote? Tell a partner.
Who did the old voting rules leave out? What did it take to change them?
Should it be easy or hard to change a rule? Say why.
Whose voice does a high bar protect? Whose voice does it slow down?

urn:const:us:mo:art-09:sec-01a.heading: Education
urn:const:us:mo:art-09:sec-01a.text: A general diffusion of knowledge and intelligence being essential to the preservation of the rights and liberties of the people, the general assembly shall establish and maintain free public schools for the gratuitous instruction of all persons in this state within ages not in excess of twenty-one years as prescribed by law.
urn:const:us:mo:art-09:sec-01a.gloss_grade_5: Missouri says learning keeps people free. So the state must run free public schools that anyone up to age 21 can attend.
urn:const:us:mo:art-09:sec-01a.gloss_grade_8: An educated public protects everyone’s rights and freedom. So the constitution requires the state to establish and maintain free public schools, open to everyone up to age twenty-one.

urn:const:us:mo:art-03:sec-49.heading: Legislative Department
urn:const:us:mo:art-03:sec-49.text: The people reserve power to propose and enact or reject laws and amendments to the constitution by the initiative, independent of the general assembly, and also reserve power to approve or reject by referendum any act of the general assembly, except as hereinafter provided.
urn:const:us:mo:art-03:sec-49.section_heading: Reservation of power to enact and reject laws.
urn:const:us:mo:art-03:sec-49.gloss_grade_5: The people keep two powers for themselves. They can write a new law and put it to a vote. They can also vote yes or no on a law the lawmakers passed.
urn:const:us:mo:art-03:sec-49.gloss_grade_8: The people keep two powers. By initiative, they can propose a law or an amendment and pass it at the ballot. By referendum, they can approve or reject a law the general assembly passed.

urn:const:us:mo:art-05:sec-25a.text: Whenever a vacancy shall occur in the office of judge of any of the following courts of this state, to wit: The supreme court, the court of appeals, or in the office of circuit or associate circuit judge within the city of St. Louis and Jackson county, the governor shall fill such vacancy by appointing one of three persons possessing the qualifications for such office, who shall be nominated and whose names shall be submitted to the governor by a nonpartisan judicial commission established and organized as hereinafter provided. If the governor fails to appoint any of the nominees within sixty days after the list of nominees is submitted, the nonpartisan judicial commission making the nomination shall appoint one of the nominees to fill the vacancy.
urn:const:us:mo:art-05:sec-25a.section_heading: Nonpartisan selection of judges — courts subject to plan — appointments to fill vacancies.
urn:const:us:mo:art-05:sec-25a.gloss_grade_5: When a judge's job opens up, a special group picks three people who could do it. The governor must choose one of those three.
urn:const:us:mo:art-05:sec-25a.gloss_grade_8: When a judge's seat on certain courts opens up, a nonpartisan commission picks three candidates. The governor must appoint one of the three.

urn:const:us:nh:art-83:sec-01.citation: New Hampshire Constitution, Part Second, Article 83

urn:const:us:va:art-03:sec-14.citation: Virginia Constitution of 1830, Article III, Section 14 (superseded)
urn:const:us:va:art-03:sec-14.teacher_note_8_10: This is an old rule from long ago. It let only some men vote. Your teacher can tell you more.

urn:const:us:mo:art-08:sec-02.text: Only citizens of the United States, including occupants of soldiers' and sailors' homes, over the age of eighteen who are residents of this state and of the political subdivision in which they offer to vote are entitled to vote at all elections by the people, if the election is one for which registration is required if they are registered within the time prescribed by law, or if the election is one for which registration is not required, if they have been residents of the political subdivision in which they offer to vote for thirty days next preceding the election for which they offer to vote: Provided however, no person who has a guardian of his or her estate or person by reason of mental incapacity, appointed by a court of competent jurisdiction and no person who is involuntarily confined in a mental institution pursuant to an adjudication of a court of competent jurisdiction shall be entitled to vote, and persons convicted of felony, or crime connected with the exercise of the right of suffrage may be excluded by law from voting.
urn:const:us:mo:art-08:sec-02.gloss_grade_5: You can vote in Missouri if you are a citizen of the United States, you are 18 or older, and you live here. The section also says when someone cannot vote.
urn:const:us:mo:art-08:sec-02.gloss_grade_8: Voters must be United States citizens, at least eighteen, and residents of Missouri and their district. The section also lists times when a person cannot vote, such as while serving a felony sentence.

urn:const:us:mo:art-12:sec-02b.text: All amendments proposed by the general assembly or by the initiative shall be submitted to the electors for their approval or rejection by official ballot title as may be provided by law, on a separate ballot without party designation, at the next general election, or at a special election called by the governor prior thereto, at which he may submit any of the amendments. No such proposed amendment shall contain more than one amended and revised article of this constitution, or one new article which shall not contain more than one subject and matters properly connected therewith. If possible, each proposed amendment shall be published once a week for two consecutive weeks in two newspapers of different political faith in each county, the last publication to be not more than thirty nor less than fifteen days next preceding the election. If there be but one newspaper in any county, publication for four consecutive weeks shall be made. If a majority of the votes cast thereon is in favor of any amendment, the same shall take effect at the end of thirty days after the election. More than one amendment at the same election shall be so submitted as to enable the electors to vote on each amendment separately.
urn:const:us:mo:art-12:sec-02b.section_heading: Submission of amendments proposed by general assembly or by the initiative.
urn:const:us:mo:art-12:sec-02b.gloss_grade_5: A change goes to the voters at the next big election. Each change is voted on by itself. If more than half the votes say yes, it starts thirty days later.
urn:const:us:mo:art-12:sec-02b.gloss_grade_8: Proposed amendments go on the ballot at the next general election, each voted on separately and each limited to one subject. If a majority of the votes cast on it say yes, it takes effect thirty days later.

urn:const:us:nh:art-100:sec-01.citation: New Hampshire Constitution, Part Second, Article 100

urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-05.heading: Bill of Rights
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-05.text: That all men and women have a natural and indefeasible right to worship Almighty God according to the dictates of their own consciences; that no human authority can control or interfere with the rights of conscience; that no person shall, on account of his or her religious persuasion or belief, be rendered ineligible to any public office or trust or profit in this state, be disqualified from testifying or serving as a juror, or be molested in his or her person or estate; that to secure a citizen's right to acknowledge Almighty God according to the dictates of his or her own conscience, neither the state nor any of its political subdivisions shall establish any official religion, nor shall a citizen's right to pray or express his or her religious beliefs be infringed; that the state shall not coerce any person to participate in any prayer or other religious activity, but shall ensure that any person shall have the right to pray individually or corporately in a private or public setting so long as such prayer does not result in disturbance of the peace or disruption of a public meeting or assembly; that citizens as well as elected officials and employees of the state of Missouri and its political subdivisions shall have the right to pray on government premises and public property so long as such prayers abide within the same parameters placed upon any other free speech under similar circumstances; that the General Assembly and the governing bodies of political subdivisions may extend to ministers, clergypersons, and other individuals the privilege to offer invocations or other prayers at meetings or sessions of the General Assembly or governing bodies; that students may express their beliefs about religion in written and oral assignments free from discrimination based on the religious content of their work; that no student shall be compelled to perform or participate in academic assignments or educational presentations that violate his or her religious beliefs; that the state shall ensure public school students their right to free exercise of religious expression without interference, as long as such prayer or other expression is private and voluntary, whether individually or corporately, and in a manner that is not disruptive and as long as such prayers or expressions abide within the same parameters placed upon any other free speech under similar circumstances; and, to emphasize the right to free exercise of religious expression, that all free public schools receiving state appropriations shall display, in a conspicuous and legible manner, the text of the Bill of Rights of the Constitution of the United States; but this section shall not be construed to expand the rights of prisoners in state or local custody beyond those afforded by the laws of the United States, excuse acts of licentiousness, nor to justify practices inconsistent with the good order, peace or safety of the state, or with the rights of others.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-05.teacher_note_8_10: This rule is about faith and prayer. Read it together with your teacher.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-05.section_heading: Religious freedom — liberty of conscience and belief — limitations — right to pray — academic religious freedoms and prayer.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-05.gloss_grade_5: Everyone can follow their own faith, or none at all. The state cannot pick a church for you or punish your beliefs. Your beliefs do not let you break fair laws.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-05.gloss_grade_8: Everyone may worship, or not, by their own conscience. The state cannot control belief or favor one faith. This liberty does not excuse acts that break laws protecting peace and safety.

urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-08.heading: Bill of Rights
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-08.text: That no law shall be passed impairing the freedom of speech, no matter by what means communicated: that every person shall be free to say, write or publish, or otherwise communicate whatever he will on any subject, being responsible for all abuses of that liberty; and that in all suits and prosecutions for libel or slander the truth thereof may be given in evidence; and in suits and prosecutions for libel the jury, under the direction of the court, shall determine the law and the facts.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-08.section_heading: Freedom of speech — evidence of truth in defamation actions — province of jury.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-08.gloss_grade_5: You are free to say and write what you think. No law can take that away. But you still answer for what you say.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-08.gloss_grade_8: No law may limit free speech, in any form. Every person may speak, write, or publish their views. Each person still answers for abusing that liberty.

urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-09.heading: Bill of Rights
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-09.text: That the people have the right peaceably to assemble for their common good, and to apply to those invested with the powers of government for redress of grievances by petition or remonstrance.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-09.section_heading: Rights of peaceable assembly and petition.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-09.gloss_grade_5: People can gather in peace for a shared cause. They can also ask the state to fix something that is wrong.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-09.gloss_grade_8: The people may gather peaceably for their common good. They may also petition the government to correct wrongs.

urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-14.heading: Bill of Rights
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-14.text: That the courts of justice shall be open to every person, and certain remedy afforded for every injury to person, property or character, and that right and justice shall be administered without sale, denial or delay.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-14.section_heading: Open courts — certain remedies — justice without sale, denial or delay.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-14.gloss_grade_5: The courts are open to every person. If someone harms you, you can ask a court for help. Justice cannot be sold or slowed on purpose.
urn:const:us:mo:art-01:sec-14.gloss_grade_8: Courts must stay open to every person, with a remedy for every injury to person, property, or character. Justice may not be sold, denied, or delayed.

urn:const:us:mo:art-04:sec-01.heading: Executive Department
urn:const:us:mo:art-04:sec-01.text: The supreme executive power shall be vested in a governor.
urn:const:us:mo:art-04:sec-01.gloss_grade_5: The state's top power to carry out the laws belongs to the governor.
urn:const:us:mo:art-04:sec-01.gloss_grade_8: The supreme executive power, the power to carry out the laws, belongs to the governor.

urn:const:us:mo:art-10:sec-01.heading: Taxation
urn:const:us:mo:art-10:sec-01.text: The taxing power may be exercised by the general assembly for state purposes, and by counties and other political subdivisions under power granted to them by the general assembly for county, municipal and other corporate purposes.
urn:const:us:mo:art-10:sec-01.section_heading: Taxing power — exercise by state and local governments.
urn:const:us:mo:art-10:sec-01.gloss_grade_5: The state's lawmakers can collect taxes for the state. Counties and towns can collect taxes too, if the lawmakers let them.
urn:const:us:mo:art-10:sec-01.gloss_grade_8: The general assembly may tax for state purposes. Counties and other local governments may tax only under power the general assembly grants them.
